Menus that reorder themselves from page to page force people to relearn the site every click. Repeated navigation should keep its relative order.
Render the same header and footer links in the same order on every page.
Reorder or hide primary links per page without reason.
Phone numbers, chat widgets and contact links should sit in the same place on every page, so people who struggle can find help quickly.
Keep the help link or number in the same header or footer position on all pages.
Move the contact route around by page type.
/* phone in header on home, footer on others */
Deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and anyone watching muted on a train, rely on captions for the speech and meaningful sounds in a video.
Add a WebVTT track with accurate captions and set default for the main language.
Rely on auto-generated captions without review, or burn them in with no track.
Podcasts and voice clips need a transcript so deaf users and anyone who cannot play sound can still read the content.
Publish a transcript on the same page or one link away.
Autoplaying Audio Has a Stop Control
Sound that plays for more than three seconds fights with screen reader speech. Users need to pause it or set its volume separately.
Do not autoplay audio; if you must, give an immediate pause control near the top of the page.
A screen reader announces a cell's row and column headers only when the table marks them with th and scope. Without them a grid of numbers is meaningless.
Use th with scope, a caption, and keep layout out of tables.
Style td cells to look like headers.
A custom control needs name, role and state exposed to assistive tech. Native button, select and input give that for free; ARIA only describes, it adds no behaviour.
Reach for the native element first; add ARIA only for patterns HTML lacks, and follow the APG keyboard model.
Put role='button' on a div without tabindex, key handling and state.
Hiding a link or button from the accessibility tree while it can still take focus leaves keyboard users on a control that is announced as nothing.
Use inert or hidden on whole off-screen panels so they leave both the tab order and the tree.
Set aria-hidden='true' on a container that holds links.
A screen reader reads source order. If CSS places the price before the name visually but after it in the source, the sequence reads wrongly.
Order the source as it should be read and use grid areas for placement.
Use order or absolute positioning to reverse content that depends on sequence.
Instructions Do Not Rely on Shape or Position
'Press the round button on the right' means nothing to someone who cannot see the layout.
Refer to controls by their visible label.
Describe controls by colour, shape or location only.
Press the green button on the right.
Real Text, Not Images of Text
Text rendered as an image will not resize, reflow, restyle or translate. Logos are the exception.
Set text in HTML and style it with CSS.
Export headings or offers as banners.
Blocking zoom stops low-vision users from enlarging content on a phone, and fails resize text.
Use width=device-width, initial-scale=1 and nothing that caps the scale.
Moving focus onto a field must not submit, navigate or open a new window. Surprises disorient screen reader and keyboard users.
Change context only on explicit activation such as Enter or a click on a button.
Auto-submit when a field receives focus.
Changing a select or radio should not move the user to another page unless they were told it would.
Add an explicit Go button, or state the behaviour before the control.
Navigate in a select's change handler.
More Than One Way to Find Pages
People find content differently: menu, search, sitemap, links. On sites with many pages, offering two or more routes helps.
Provide navigation plus search or a sitemap link.
Rely on one hierarchical menu alone.
In a single-page app, a route change does not reload the page, so focus and the screen reader cursor stay on the old link. Users hear nothing happen.
After navigation, move focus to the new h1 or main and update the document title.
Swap the view and leave focus on the clicked link.
Headings and form labels should say what the section or field is. Vague ones make skimming with assistive tech slow.
Write headings that describe their section and labels that name the field.
Long documents are easier to scan when sections are broken up with headings.
Give each section its own heading.
Run a long article as one block.
An icon or label that means search in one place should not mean filter in another.
Use one icon and one name per function across the site.
Rename or redraw the same control on different pages.
Enhanced Contrast Where It Is Cheap
The AAA level asks for 7:1 for body text. Long-form reading, older audiences and outdoor use benefit from it.
Aim for 7:1 on body text on content-heavy and care or public service sites.
Stop at the bare minimum on long reading pages.
If the visuals carry information not in the speech, blind users miss it. Describe it in a separate audio track or the narration.
Narrate on-screen actions in the script or add a described version.
Show steps visually with silent narration.
When a session expires and the user signs in again, the work they had should still be there.
Persist form state in the session or local storage before redirecting to sign-in.
Redirect to login and drop the half-complete form.
Unrequested pop-ups and notifications interrupt focus and reading. Let people delay or suppress non-urgent ones.
Batch non-urgent messages and offer a setting to defer them.
Open an offer modal while the user is mid-task.
